articles.title: How to sustain research?
articles.content: IN terms of urgent and important problems requiring resolution, Pakistan’s education sector is the real frontier. With some 26 million five- to 16-year-olds out of school, a lack of universal enrolment, high dropout rates, and the poor quality of education provided to most of those lucky enough to be enrolled, could any issue be more important? Pakistan has a very young population; we are still growing at 2.4 per cent every year. This means that approximately 6m children are added to the population annually. In more developed societies, the frontiers are about ageing populations and health. In Pakistan, they are about children, their schooling and health; young people and their education and skills; and early employment opportunities. All this implies that Pakistan provides a research frontier for those interested in education. And we need a lot of research. We face big questions and need good answers: how can we provide education to millions; how do we improve the quality of education; how do we manage private versus public schools; how do we recruit, train, and support teachers; how do we govern and manage schools and systems better; how do we ensure good curricula, books, assessments, teaching, etc? The list is long; we need good research to answer all these questions and more. But, historically — and even today — education research has not been a priority area for funding. First, the education sector, as a whole, has always been underfunded. Even in better days, the state never spent more than 2pc of GDP on education; currently, we are at less than 1pc. Within this, one can imagine what funding for research would be and what, within research funding, funding for education research must have been. Second, there are strong biases in research funding agencies, such as the Higher Education Commission, for research in science and technology as against research in the social sciences, humanities and the arts. The general thinking is that Pakistan needs engineers and technologists — and thus research in science and technology for development. Research in the social sciences, humanities, and the arts is not seen as important or needed, nor is it viewed as providing the returns that society needs. Historically, research done on education in Pakistan was conducted either locally — with smaller budgets and samples — by academics and students in university education programmes, or by foreign academics and academics based abroad. The latter had higher budgets. A lot of the research was funded by multilateral and bilateral agencies such as the World Bank, DFID (now FCDO — the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office), USAID, GIZ, etc. A lot of the local research was not published internationally, while international work did little or nothing to develop local capacity. Some good partnerships developed between local and international academics, but these were rare and tended not to last beyond the life of the project. Education research has not been a priority area for funding. It has been interesting to follow the Data and Research in Education — Research Consortium (DARE-RC) in this context. This FCDO-funded programme, due to end by December, tried to change the existing equilibrium. The main ingredients of change were the following: a) it encouraged local researchers to apply for competitive funding; b) it encouraged collaborations across local institutions; c) it encouraged collaborations across local and international academics and institutions as well; d) it committed to making all data public; and e) it insisted on quality outputs that should be published internationally. More than 40 different studies were commissioned; many of them have been completed and their reports and policy briefs are available. Some of the early studies have already been slated for publication in international journals, while many are in the process of being submitted. Some will be appearing in a special issue of an international journal. Many interesting partnerships have been created among local universities, between universities and research institutions, between local and international researchers, and between local and international universities. This has led to quite a bit of capacity building, and has provided each project with junior research assistants. Quite a few people have been trained and mentored over the last few years. There has been considerable interaction with policymakers and the wider public, with one or two DARE-RC events held every couple of weeks this year. DARE-RC has even started a yearly conference on education. The second edition is at the end of the month in Lahore. But there are issues too. As DARE-RC winds down and the funding ends, it appears that, given the new global funding realities, FCDO is not going to support such programmes anymore. What happens to the gains made? Will the collaborations be sustained? Will someone take over the yearly conference? Will the fora created for capacity building and sharing research continue beyond DARE-RC funding? Will the sharing of data for research continue? Will cooperation between researchers and policymakers continue? Or will it lapse as it has on previous occasions? Will the government, federal or provincial education departments, or HEC take on the role of research funder? The research has been very policy-focused and has helped in critical areas such as teacher recruitment and licensing, inclusive education, improved teaching and learning in classrooms, education and support for children with disabilities, and curricula and textbook improvements. Do departments see value in such research, and will they provide support for sustaining and expanding the networks that have been created? Research is the backbone of progress, but quality research is expensive, hard to do, and even harder to sustain. We urgently need a lot of high-quality research in education. Recent investments, through DARE-RC in particular, have provided insights and lessons on how networks capable of producing the high-quality research needed to improve education outcomes can be created. But will these gains be sustainable beyond the life of the project? What will continue and what will not? A lot depends on whether the HEC or the education departments come forward to support and expand the current networks. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: The bureaucratic bargain
articles.content: IN an earlier column on these pages, ‘Inefficient by design’, I had argued that many of Pakistan’s economic distortions persist not because policymakers misunderstand their costs, but because they benefit groups capable of defending them. That argument raises a further question: what institutional machinery sustains this distribution of benefits? One answer is the bureaucracy. The answer begins with bureaucracy’s origins. The British did not construct the colonial administrative state to maximise productivity or deliver public services. Its primary tasks were revenue collection, territorial control, and political order. The district collector embodied this design: an appointed officer with extensive executive and revenue powers, answerable to the colonial government rather than the people he governed. Information flowed upwards; instructions flowed downwards. Concentrating authority in a small administrative elite allowed the British to govern a vast population at relatively low cost. Much of this design survived independence. Pakistan and India retained powerful generalist civil services recruited through competitive examinations. These may identify intelligence and diligence, but they cannot establish expertise in public finance, urban management, health systems, industrial policy, or digital regulation. Yet the governing assumption remains that success in a single examination, followed by general training, prepares an officer to move across such specialised fields, often supervising professionals who have spent their careers working in them. This is not an argument against meritocratic recruitment or the need for administrative coordination. Generalists have a role in both. The problem arises when generalist status confers authority over specialised knowledge. A capable administrator is not automatically a capable regulator, economist, engineer or public-health manager. Too often, specialists provide the expertise while generalists retain the final decision. Frequent transfers limit opportunities to develop sectoral expertise, while promotion within a centralised hierarchy can reward navigating the system rather than improving the performance of the institutions being managed. Why does an arrangement that imposes such costs on the economy prove so resistant to reform? Why does this matter for development? Institutions determine who controls economic decisions and whose interests those decisions serve. When officials exercise broad authority without bearing the costs of their decisions, their incentives can diverge from those of investors and workers. Such institutional arrangements can outlive the purposes for which they were created. For example, economists Banerjee and Iyer showed that areas in India where the British assigned land rights to landlords subsequently experienced lower agricultural investment and productivity than those where rights went to cultivators. Their study concerns land tenure, not bureaucratic recruitment, but illustrates a broader principle: rules that allocate economic power also shape incentives to invest and produce. The question is how the inherited concentration of administrative authority affects these incentives today. The contemporary mechanism is discretion. A business seeking a land title, an industrial permit, construction approval, or regulatory clearance must navigate a series of administrative decisions. Regulation can serve legitimate purposes; arbitrary dependence on permission does not. When officials can delay, reinterpret or selectively enforce rules, access to the state acquires economic value. Firms devote resources to connections and intermediaries that could otherwise finance technology, workers or new products. The costs are unevenly distributed. Established firms can afford legal teams, influence, and prolonged delays; new entrants often cannot. Predictable rules encourage investment and experimentation, while discretionary permissions favour insiders. The result is more than petty corruption or administrative delay. It distorts the allocation of capital and talent, weakens competition and holds back productivity. Why does an arrangement that imposes such costs on the economy prove so resistant to reform? Because its costs are dispersed across businesses, investors, and citizens, while the benefits of discretion are concentrated among those who exercise or influence it. The authority to grant an approval, interpret a rule or allow an exemption is itself valuable. Those who control such decisions have little incentive to surrender them. This creates a political bargain. Bureaucrats derive influence from the authority attached to their offices; politicians gain leverage by influencing how that authority is exercised. Appointments and transfers can reward cooperation and penalise resistance. Desirable postings, in turn, can give officials influence well beyond their formal responsibilities. The two groups may compete over particular decisions, but their interests converge in preserving the system that makes those decisions valuable. Reform threatens not merely administrative procedures but an established distribution of political and economic power. This is not a claim that every official is corrupt; it is an argument about the incentives embedded in the office. Reform, therefore, should not be reduced to new examinations, training courses, or digital platforms. These may improve administrative processes without changing who controls decisions, how that power is rewarded or to whom it is accountable. Pakistan’s development debate rightly asks how to raise investment, exports, and productivity. It should also ask who has the authority to obstruct them, how that authority is rewarded, and why its holders would surrender it. The answer requires more than building bureaucratic capacity; it requires limiting arbitrary discretion, creating space for specialist expertise, and making officials accountable for outcomes. We inherited a state designed to control economic life. The enduring constraint is not simply the bureaucracy’s lack of capacity, but a political bargain that rewards the exercise of administrative power at the expense of economic development. The writer is an associate professor of economics at the Lahore School of Economics.
articles.author: Waqar Wadho

articles.title: Outdated practices
articles.content: MANY societies try to improve their quality of life. Some are successful in their efforts while others face difficulties. The main impediments to improvement include some outdated practices that ought to be uprooted. It can take centuries to convince people that certain traditions or practices are no longer viable. Take slavery. Even today, though the world thinks it has eradicated the practice, people still live in bondage in many areas. Usually, practices entrenched in people’s minds do not fade away unless concerted efforts are made. In centuries past, it was common in some cultures to give away females in exchange for cattle or food. Sati, the Hindu tradition of burning the widow alive on the funeral pyre of her husband, was prevalent until stopped during the British Raj. For the smooth running of society, the process of improving well-being and the quality of life for individuals and communities continues through enhanced social structures, legislation, relationships, and institutions. It focuses on issues such as education, healthcare, and the quality of life. The aim is to create an inclusive society that promotes social justice and cohesion. Thus, a country’s prospects hinge on eradicating anti-people practices that have affected weaker segments such as women more than any other section of society. Today, Pakistan is plagued by many strange practices that also violate human rights. The practices are usually driven by anti-women feelings. The worst part is that they are accepted by many in society. The cause of these ingrained ills in our system is perhaps the result of an antediluvian mindset, which believes that a woman is a saleable commodity. This goes against the teachings of Islam. Allah says in the Holy Quran: “O mankind! Be dutiful to your Lord, Who created you from a single soul… .” (4:1) We are plagued by customs that violate human rights. And yet, in many households, the birth of a daughter is not welcomed. When the daughter grows up, the parents impose strict restrictions on her. She cannot go outside to play and her movements remain under watch. When the girl is about to get married, the demands of the groom’s family for dowry can be a terrifying ordeal for her family. Society needs to free itself from such a rigid and retrogressive mindset. Among the long list of anti-social practices, the issue of child marriage is often highlighted by the media. It is a grave social issue that violates a girl’s rights and undermines the very fabric of society. Its harmful outcome extends beyond the lives of the girls affected, and has an adverse impact on entire communities and economies. But the most immediate and devastating impact of child marriage is on the personal growth and well-being of underage girls. Girls suffer far more than boys in this regard, with many being married off to much older men by their families in line with strange customs or because of economic stress. Marriage at a tender age robs girls of their childhood and innocence, forcing them into responsibilities that they are neither mentally nor emotionally prepared for. Similarly, the practice of so-called honour killing is devastating. It involves the murder of a family member — mostly women and girls — by their male relatives who believe the victim has brought shame or ‘dishonour’ to the family, often by marrying of their own free will. The violence is typically tied to primitive anti-women codes and social traditions, which need to be uprooted. Moreover, practices such as wani and swara, predominant in Pakistan’s tribal cultures, involve giving away minor girls or women to settle bloody disputes. This needs to be stopped altogether. As does the practice of ‘marriage’ with the Holy Quran. Possession of her due share in inheritance is the most effective way to make a woman financially secure. Furthermore, girls’ education should be presented as a religious obligation; in fact, the need for it should be amplified from all platforms. Regressive practices must be termed national handicaps in the process of development. A country cannot hope to progress when such a large number of harmful and outdated practices exist, which deny education, healthcare, and development to a vast number of citizens. Though laws banning many of these outdated practices exist, they need strict enforcement. Thus, the real challenge lies in their implementation, which remains weak and inconsistent. In places, it is virtually non-existent. If these scourges are to be eradicated, it requires more than lip service. It demands political will, community engagement, and above all, recognition that progress cannot coexist with practices that hurt society’s development. The change must begin now, before another generation is lost to silence. The writer is an educationist with an interest in religion.
articles.author: Amin Valliani

articles.title: Welfarism is dead
articles.content: PARADED as amongst the greatest achievements of ‘advanced’ capitalist countries in the post-World War II period, the welfare state epitomised an era of widespread social prosperity. The mass of people in Western Europe, North America, and Australasia was largely guaranteed public education, healthcare, water, electricity, and other material needs. Working-age populations either found work in bustling manufacturing industries or received significant unemployment benefits. The anti-communist US ideologue, Walt Rostow, boasted that the ‘West’ had successfully entered the age of high mass consumption. Today, as massprotestsrock France, the welfare state can officially be pronounced dead. The convulsions were triggered by high school and university students demanding accountability for the rapidly deteriorating and underfunded education sector. The demise extends to all spheres of life, and to all parts of the so-called developed world. The welfare state itself was not a gift from above but a compulsion forced upon ruling classes of Western countries petrified of working-class populations at home and colonised people demanding self-rule in Asia and Africa. The fear was that the masses would be taken in by the irrepressible appeal of Soviet, and later, Chinese socialism. Seen thus, the welfare state represented a historic compromise between capital and labour. The former accepted regulation of profits, progressive taxation, and limits on its political power; the latter took on the role of an empowered citizenry that would eschew revolutionary politics. It is no surprise that the unravelling of this capital-labour compact coincided to a significant extent with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War. The balance of class forces within Western societies had already started to shift with the emergence of what later became known as neoliberalism in the late 1970s, but the die was cast by the end of actually existing socialism. It has been a slow death, because welfare apparatuses do not disappear overnight; neither do people’s expectations of the state. Indeed, what is happening in France today is itself a reflection that the mass of the people deeply imbibed ideas of citizenship during the era of welfarism. Compared to our society, students, workers, and other social forces in countries like France are still well-organised and possess the ability and will to rock the system. Nevertheless, the unleashing of neoliberal capital and the attendant rollback of public funding in health, education, and other public infrastructure have had devastating effects. Stagnating real incomes, growing inequality, and an overall decline in social well-being have been feasted on by hate-mongering right-wing forces, while entities like the British Labour Party and French Socialist Party have totally abandoned the left project. The shameful retreat of social democratic parties aside, the welfare state will not return because the historical conjuncture that spawned it is over. The reconstruction of war-ravaged Britain and France from the late 1940s was funded by Washington through the so-called Marshall Plan; post-Nazi West Germany was also given an economic foothold in world trade because of US largesse. The US empire is no longer willing to prop up Europe; it is also drastically cutting aid to the so-called developing world. It’s worth being reminded that the zenith of the welfare state in ‘advanced’ capitalist countries was coeval with either aid dependency, violent coups, or imperialist wars in the erstwhile Third World. Think Pakistan under Ayub Khan, or Vietnam, the Congo and Chile. A few Third World countries broke with the dominant trend, notably the East Asian ‘developmental state’. Some, like South Korea, benefited from being central to Washington’s Cold War designs, their infant industries given preferential access to the US market. But state apparatuses were authoritarian, and there were fewer concessions made to labouring classes by capitalist interests in comparison to the Western prototype. We in Pakistan have never really had a welfarist interregnum. When socialism was a mass ideology in the 1960s and 1970s, governing regimes adopted a few tangible policies like land reforms and nationalisation. But the state remained colonial in its orientation and was never fully subdued to the public interest. Today, like many of its counterparts, the Pakistani state couldn’t care less about the masses’ welfare. Profit and repression are its only concerns. When mass protests do erupt, structural change remains elusive. A new era of mass prosperity to transcend the historical inheritance of the capitalist world system requires both ideology and organisation. Only then can we force the state and capital into retreat. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: Nuclear uncertainty
articles.content: CONSIDERING the poor state of bilateral relations between Pakistan and India, there is always a possibility of miscalculating a situation, especially in the absence of regular contact. These concerns take on greater importance in the nuclear domain. In this regard, officials associated with Pakistan’s nuclear programme have rightly warned that India’s reported attempt to alter the strategic balance has heightened risks of escalation in South Asia. Speaking at a conference in Islamabad, retired Lt-Gen Khalid Kidwai, adviser to the National Command Authority, highlighted a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, which said that India had deployed nuclear warheads on a submarine as part of “deterrence patrols”. He also cited New Delhi’s lack of advance notification for ballistic missile tests. The official observed that these developments cast doubt on India’s no-first-use policy, and were seen as an “irresponsible escalatory transition” towards nuclear asymmetry. Lack of coordination between nuclear states creates great unknowns, and such a situation is untenable in a neighbourhood as volatile as South Asia. It should be remembered that it was only last year that Pakistan and Indiaconfrontedeach other on the battlefield, illustrating how quickly matters can escalate. In such an atmosphere, India’s apparent attempts to alter the strategic balance are cause for serious concern. As Lt-Gen Kidwai pointed out, Pakistan may “review and reconsider” its deployment options, while reminding New Delhi of this country’s full spectrum deterrence policy. With matters frozen in the political and diplomatic spheres, it will take military-to-military engagement to prevent miscalculation in the strategic sphere. This can be carried out through the directors general military operations hotline, or via other appropriate channels. India’s political class — as well as military officials — has issued jingoistic statements targeting Pakistan. There is certainly no room for such bluster where the issue of nuclear weapons is concerned. To ward off any potential catastrophe, the situation must be handled in a rational manner and lines of communication need to be kept open to ensure conventional or nuclear signals are not misconstrued. India should halt its highly provocative nuclear-armed submarine patrols and engage with Pakistan to ensure there are no misunderstandings, particularly in the strategic sphere. Regular diplomatic engagement may seem distant at this juncture, but contact between the defence command structures should continue, while de-escalation mechanisms should also be maintained. Most of all, India should give up its rash attitude and approach the issue with maturity if it wants to reduce tensions and advance regional peace.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Auto illusion
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S draft auto policy 2026-31 is ambitious in its targets and directionless in its strategy. It promises electrification, export growth, greater competition, and stronger local manufacturing. However, some of its most consequential incentives threaten to undermine these very goals. The proposed policy aims to generate $6bn in exports over five years, while reducing import tariffs and promoting ‘new’ energy vehicles. These are sensible goals. But targets cannot be achieved without a credible strategy. The draft sent to the cabinet for its approval needs a fundamental rethink before it becomes policy. Consider the proposed sales tax of 9pc on plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, against 18pc under the standard rate. By granting PHEVs a substantial tax advantage, the government is effectively treating vehicles that continue to largely depend on petrol as a preferred route to electrification. This is difficult to reconcile with the stated aim of cutting the oil import bill and reducing transport emissions. A battery EV, by contrast, eliminates petrol consumption altogether. Giving PHEVs generous tax concessions without clear performance conditions risks encouraging consumers to remain tied to fossil fuels. Sadly, the government appears to have yielded to pressure from hybrid carmakers rather than applying a consistent technological framework. If electrification is the intention, incentives should favour only those vehicles that deliver the greatest reduction in petroleum consumption and emissions. The export ambition is also debatable. The policy envisages a sharp rise in vehicle and parts exports — without a production strategy. Chinese and Korean auto producers have not authorised their Pakistani partners to make or assemble their brands here for international markets. Unless the government secures commitments to use Pakistan as an export base, the targets are wishful planning. Lowering taxes on Chinese vehicles while assemblers keep relying on imported components could entrench low-value assembly. Local vendors would face mounting pressure from cheaper imported parts, and those struggling at home cannot become exporters. Tariff liberalisation is not entirely misguided. However, the government must distinguish between protection that sustains inefficiency and a time-bound framework that helps producers reach scale. Currently, the policy risks subsidising petrol-dependent technology, wiping out local autoparts makers, and promising exports the industry cannot deliver.
